title: A blessing for each food
hook: bread, grain, wine, tree fruit, earth fruit and everything else each have their own blessing

segments.voice: Yesterday, baruch, the six words that open almost every blessing. Your line was six words before anything. Now, what comes after the six? Day one hundred thirteen.

A kitchen table: an apple, a strawberry, a slice of bread, a cookie, a glass of wine and a piece of cheese. Ask someone who keeps the blessings to bless them. They won't say the same thing six times. They'll say six different endings. The apple gets one. The strawberry gets another, and it's not the same as the apple. The cookie and the bread aren't the same either, though they're both made from flour. It sounds like a quiz. It's really a way of looking at what's on your plate. Today: hamotzi, and its cousins.
screen: `SIX FOODS ON A KITCHEN TABLE.` → `SIX DIFFERENT ENDINGS.` → `A WAY OF LOOKING AT YOUR PLATE.`

segments.voice: After the six opening words, each food gets its own ending. Bread: hamotzi lechem min ha'aretz, who brings forth bread from the earth. The words come from a psalm that says, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, God makes things grow "to bring forth bread out of the earth." Other grain foods, like cake, cookies or pasta: borei minei mezonot, who creates kinds of nourishment. Wine and grape juice: borei pri hagafen, who creates the fruit of the vine. Fruit from a tree: borei pri ha'etz. Fruit and vegetables from the ground: borei pri ha'adamah, the fruit of the earth. And everything else, cheese, eggs, water, candy: shehakol nihyeh bidvaro, by whose word all things came to be. So the apple gets tree, and the strawberry gets earth, because it grows on a low plant. A banana, surprisingly, gets earth too, since the plant it grows on isn't a tree in the rabbis' sense: it doesn't keep its trunk year to year. The Talmud asks why bless food at all, and it notices two verses that seem to disagree. One psalm says: "The earth is the LORD'S, and the fulness thereof." Another says: "the earth hath He given to the children of men." Which is it? The Talmud's answer: before the blessing, it's God's. After the blessing, it's been given to you. Enjoying food without a blessing, the Talmud says, is like making personal use of something set aside for the Temple. The blessing is how the food changes hands. And the endings make you look closely: where did this grow, on a tree, in the ground, from grain? An apple and a strawberry, side by side on one plate, end up with different words.
screen: `WHO BRINGS FORTH BREAD.` · `TREE, EARTH, VINE, GRAIN.` · `EVERYTHING ELSE: BY HIS WORD.` · `BEFORE THE BLESSING, IT'S GOD'S.` · then, large: `THE EARTH IS THE LORD'S.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: match a blessing to one food today. Let's warm up now. Settle, and breathe. Picture the next thing you'll eat. Now trace it back. Did it grow on a tree, like an apple or an orange? In the ground, like a potato, a tomato, a strawberry? From grain, like bread or pasta? Or is it something else, like cheese or an egg? Name its category, tree, earth, grain, bread, vine or everything else. If you pray, you can say its blessing when you eat it. If not, just pause and name where it came from. The bell holds the time.
Hamotzi. Who brings forth bread from the earth: the blessing over bread, one of six endings, each food with its own word.
Your line: each food has its word. Today, before you eat, name where the food grew, even silently. Day one hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: Before eating, observant Jews say the blessing that matches the food, bread, other grain foods, wine, tree fruit, earth fruit, or everything else, and the bread blessing covers the rest of a meal with bread.

fork.setup: you're one of the rabbis. one psalm says the earth is the LORD's. another says the earth was given to people. how do you reconcile them?
options: before the blessing it's God's; after, it's given to you.
it belongs to whoever grew it.
fork.reveal: the Talmud's answer: the blessing is the moment of asking. before it, the food is God's; after it, it's been given to you.

original.note: Hebrew: who brings forth. the full ending is hamotzi lechem min ha'aretz, who brings forth bread from the earth.

trapdoor: what you thought: grace before meals.
what it means: six endings for six kinds of food, each naming where it came from, bread, grain, vine, tree, earth, or everything else.
what a scholar hears: Mishnah Berakhot 6:1–3 sets the categories; Berakhot 35a resolves Psalm 24:1 and 115:16 by the blessing.

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Psalm 104:14, 24:1 and 115:16.
Blessing endings transliterated and translated plainly; confirm.
Banana as ha'adamah: Shulchan Aruch OC 203:3 (Mishnah Berurah); strawberry as ha'adamah (low plant). Confirm.
Berakhot 35a: enjoying without a blessing likened to me'ilah (misusing sacred property); simplified as 'taking from something holy without asking'. Confirm.

Editor review (days 113–131): hook no longer leans on a 'Jewish grandmother' stock figure; Berakhot 35a line now says 'like making personal use of something set aside for the Temple' (closer to me'ilah) instead of 'taking without asking'; 'every meal becomes a little map of the world' uplift replaced with a concrete image.
